props.title: Brother Sun, Sister Moon
props.initialSlug: Young rebel finds faith as St. Francis of Assisi

sections.content: Brother Sun, Sister Moon (1972) represents Franco Zeffirelli's vibrant, hippie-influenced take on Saint Francis of Assisi. Coming off his acclaimed Romeo and Juliet (1968), Zeffirelli captured the counterculture zeitgeist by portraying Francis as a 13th-century flower child rejecting materialism. The film's gorgeous cinematography by Ennio Guarnieri bathes medieval Italy in golden light, while Donovan's folk soundtrack firmly plants it in the peace-and-love era. Though criticized for simplifying Francis's spiritual journey, it powerfully depicts his radical embrace of poverty and connection to nature.

sections.content: The 1970s saw several bold reinterpretations of religious figures that reflected contemporary social movements. Jesus Christ Superstar (1973) turned the Gospel into a rock opera, while Godspell (1973) reimagined Jesus's followers as hippie clowns in New York City. Like Brother Sun, Sister Moon, these films emphasized themes of social justice, simple living, and rebellion against institutional authority that resonated with young audiences questioning traditional religious structures.

Zeffirelli's approach influenced later spiritual biopics that balanced historical accuracy with modern relevance. Gandhi (1982) similarly portrayed its subject as a revolutionary advocating radical non-violence. The Last Temptation of Christ (1988) sparked controversy by humanizing Jesus through a contemporary psychological lens. These films share Brother Sun's technique of making ancient spiritual figures accessible through modern artistic sensibilities. SUBHEAD: Visual Poetry and Religious Cinema

movies.title: Francesco
movies.slug: More historically detailed portrayal of Francis of Assisi starring Mickey Rourke

sections.content: The film's lush visual style draws from both religious art and 1960s psychedelia. Like Carl Theodor Dreyer's The Passion of Joan of Arc (1928) and Roberto Rossellini's The Flowers of St. Francis (1950), Zeffirelli uses intense close-ups and natural light to create a sense of spiritual transcendence. This approach influenced later religious films like Into Great Silence (2005), which similarly emphasizes contemplative beauty and natural rhythms in depicting monastic life.
